source_text: Non pudet, inquam, non pudet fideles homines et christiani sibi nominis auctoritatem uindicantes superstitiones uanas gentilium cum spectaculis mixtas de scripturis caelestibus uindicare et diuinam, auctoritatem idololatriae conferre. nam quando id quod in honore alicuius idoli ab ethnicis agitur a fidelibus christianis spectaculo frequentatur, et idololatria gentilis asseritur et in contumeliam Dei religio uera et diuina calcatur. pudor me tenet praescriptiones eorum in hac causa et patrocinia referre. \'ubi\', inquiunt, scripta sunt ista, ubi prohibita? alioquin et auriga est Israel Helias et ante aream Dauid ipse saltauit. nabla cynaras aera tympana tibias citharas choros legimus. apostolus quoque dimicans caestus et colluctationis nostrae aduersus spiritalia nequitiae proponit certamen. rursus cum de stadio sumit exempla, coronae quoque collocat praemia. cur ergo homini christiano fideli non liceat spectare quod licuit diuinis litteris scribare\'? hoc in loco non immerito dixerim longe melius fuisse istis nullas litteras nosse quam sic litteras legere. uerba enim et exempla quae ad exhortationem euangelicae uirtutis posita sunt ad uitiorum patrocinia transferuntur: quoniam non ut spectarentur ista scripta sunt, sed ut animis nostris instantia maior excitaretur in rebus profuturis, dum tanta est apud ethnicos in rebus non profuturis.
thought_title: Scripture twisted into a defense of idolatrous shows
orientation: Novatian is refuting Christians who claim Scripture does not forbid public shows and who cite biblical examples to defend attending them.
pass_a_gloss: It is not shameful, I say, it is not shameful for faithful men and men claiming for themselves the authority of the Christian name to claim from the heavenly Scriptures the empty superstitions of the gentiles mixed with public shows and to confer divine authority upon idolatry. For when that which is done by pagans in honor of some idol is attended as a public show by faithful Christians, both gentile idolatry is asserted and true and divine religion is trampled in insult to God. Shame holds me from reporting their objections and defenses in this case. 'Where', they say, 'are these things written, where forbidden? Otherwise Elijah is also the charioteer of Israel and David himself danced before the ark. We read of nabla, cynaras, bronze instruments, drums, pipes, citharas, choruses. The apostle also, fighting with the cestus, sets before us the contest of our wrestling against spiritual forces of wickedness. Again when he takes examples from the stadium, he also sets out the prizes of the crown. Why therefore should it not be permitted to a faithful Christian man to watch what it was permitted to the divine writings to write?' In this place I would say not undeservedly that it would have been far better for these people to know no writings than to read writings in this way. For words and examples which were placed for the exhortation of evangelical virtue are transferred to the defenses of vices: since these things were not written so that they might be watched, but so that greater urgency might be stirred in our minds toward things that will profit, while so great is the urgency among pagans in things that will not profit.

pass_b_english: I say it again: it is not shameful—indeed, it is not shameful—for faithful people, for those who claim for themselves the authority of the Christian name, to defend the empty superstitions of the Gentiles mixed up with public shows by appealing to the heavenly Scriptures, and to hand over divine authority to idolatry. For when what the pagans do in honor of some idol is attended by faithful Christians as a public show, then Gentile idolatry is affirmed, and true and divine religion is trampled in contempt of God. Shame holds me back from repeating their objections and defenses in this matter. “Where,” they say, “are these things written? Where are they forbidden? After all, Elijah is the charioteer of Israel, and David himself danced before the arena. We read of harps, lyres, bronze cymbals, drums, flutes, and dances. The apostle too, fighting with the cestus, sets before us the contest of our wrestling against spiritual forces of wickedness. Again, when he takes examples from the stadium, he also sets out the prizes of the crown. Why then should a faithful Christian not be allowed to watch what the divine writings were allowed to write?” At this point I would rightly say that it would have been far better for these people to know no writings at all than to read the writings in this way. For the words and examples that were set down to stir us toward evangelical virtue are twisted into defenses of vices—since these things were not written so that they might be watched, but so that a greater urgency might be stirred in our minds toward things that profit us, seeing how great an urgency the pagans show in things that do not profit.

problems.quote: David himself danced before the ark.
problems.why: Latin says David danced before the arena (aream), not before the ark.
problems.fix: David himself danced before the arena.
problems.ruling: Latin 'aream' means arena, not ark; David danced before the arena, not the ark.

edits.old: David himself danced before the ark.
edits.new: David himself danced before the arena.

fixed: Changed 'ark' to 'arena' because the source reads 'ante aream' (before the arena), not 'ante arcam' (before the ark).

problems.quote: it is shameful—shameful—for faithful people, for those who claim for themselves the authority of the Christian name, to defend the empty superstitions of the Gentiles mixed up with public shows by appealing to the heavenly Scriptures, and to hand over divine authority to idolatry.
problems.source_quote: Non pudet, inquam, non pudet fideles homines et christiani ...
problems.why: Latin says ‘non pudet’ (it is not shameful); English reverses to ‘shameful’.
problems.fix: It is not shameful—indeed, it is not shameful—for faithful people, for those who claim for themselves the authority of the Christian name, to defend the empty superstitions of the Gentiles mixed up with public shows by appealing to the heavenly Scriptures, and to hand over divine authority to idolatry.
problems.ruling: Latin 'Non pudet' means 'it is not shameful'; English renders opposite 'it is shameful,' reversing the author's meaning.

edits.new: it is not shameful—indeed, it is not shameful—for faithful people

fixed: Negation: source 'Non pudet, inquam, non pudet' means 'It is not shameful, I say, it is not shameful'; English reversed the sense.

last_rejected.quote: I say it again: it is not shameful—indeed, it is not shameful—for faithful people
last_rejected.source_quote: Non pudet, inquam, non pudet fideles homines et christiani sibi nominis auctoritatem uindicantes superstitiones uanas gentilium cum spectaculis mixtas de scripturis caelestibus uindicare et diuinam, auctoritatem idololatriae conferre.
last_rejected.why: Source says 'it is not shameful for faithful people... to defend...' The English makes 'it is not shameful for faithful people' a standalone clause, losing the infinitive construction that specifies what is shameful.
last_rejected.fix: I say: it is not shameful—indeed, it is not shameful—for faithful people and Christians claiming the authority of their name to defend from the heavenly Scriptures the empty superstitions of the Gentiles mixed with public shows, and to attribute divine authority to idolatry.
last_rejected.ruling: English keeps infinitive 'to defend', preserving Latin sense; phrasing not a meaning loss.

last_rejected.quote: to hand over divine authority to idolatry
last_rejected.why: 'conferre' here means 'to attribute/grant,' not 'hand over.' The point is they lend divine authority to idolatry, not surrender it.
last_rejected.fix: to attribute divine authority to idolatry
last_rejected.ruling: ‘conferre’ = grant/attribute; ‘hand over’ conveys giving authority, acceptable nuance.

last_rejected.why: 'area' here refers to the threshing-floor or open space where the ark was placed (2 Sam 6), not an 'arena' in the spectacle sense, which misleads given the treatise's topic.
last_rejected.ruling: ‘ante aream’ can mean arena; translation fits context of public spectacle, not a critical shift.

last_rejected.why: 'domicans' should be 'dominans' (ruling/mastering), not 'domicans' (if read as fighting). The apostle 'mastering the cestus' proposes the contest of our wrestling.
last_rejected.fix: mastering the cestus, sets before us the contest of our wrestling
last_rejected.ruling: ‘domicans’ ambiguous; ‘fighting with the cestus’ plausible; not a clear mistranslation.
